extracted.intended_audience: Commission on the Political and Constitutional Future of Québec; policymakers, government negotiators, and international law practitioners
extracted.subtask_short: state succession asset and debt division
extracted.subtask_description: Legal guidance on the international-law rules and practical criteria for apportioning state property, public debt and pension liabilities when part of a state (Québec) secedes from a predecessor state (Canada). Analyses applicability of the 1983 Vienna Convention, customary rules, state practice, and possible bases for apportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of international law to secession
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of secession and succession of States fall within the jurisdiction of international law and are not confined to domestic law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process of a territory separating and forming a new state is governed by international law; consequences flow from that characterisation. Any analysis must therefore consider international rules (e.g., Vienna Conventions) and customary international law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession type matters (separation vs decolonization vs dissolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different forms of state succession (separation of part of an existing state, total dissolution, uniting states, decolonisation) invoke different rules and regimes under international law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Québec/Canada case is a separation of part of a state (not decolonisation), so rules applicable to newly independent states (decolonisation regimes) generally do not apply. Conventions and state practice distinguish these categories and apply different consequences (e.g., 'clean slate' vs continuity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Vienna Convention 1983 — status and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1983 Vienna Convention on Succession of States in Respect of State Property, Archives and Debts is controversial, not widely ratified, and cannot be treated as binding on non-parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not binding on many Western states, some provisions may reflect customary international law and thus be persuasive. Controversial provisions (esp. on decolonisation/newly independent states) are not directly relevant here, but other provisions may inform practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predecessor and successor freedom to agree
rubrics_metrics.description: Most international legal principles on succession are subject to agreement to the contrary by predecessor and successor states; states retain flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreements between the parties can override general stipulations. Many issues are best resolved through negotiation; examples include treaty arrangements like the UK/Irish Free State Treaty and Indian/Pakistan arrangements post-partition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial/territorialist principle for state property
rubrics_metrics.description: Public property of the predecessor state that is linked to the territory in question passes to the successor state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 8 (definition of state property) and Article 17 (immovable and movable property connected with activity in the territory) support the customary rule that public property in the territory passes to the successor. This includes local treasury balances, reserves, funds specifically allocated to the territory, savings deposits and pensions payable to persons in the territory.

rubrics_metrics.name: State property passes without compensation (subject to agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 11 provides that state property passes to the successor without compensation, unless the parties agree otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the default rule is transfer without compensation, parties can agree different arrangements (example: Article 208 Austrian Peace Treaty required valuation and crediting to Austria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of other movable property — equitable proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Other movable state property of the predecessor state not clearly linked to the territory is to pass to the successor 'in an equitable proportion' under Article 17, but this provision is controversial and may not reflect custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 17's nod to territorialism is debated; states may treat such movable property differently in practice. Agreement between parties will often determine outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of state debts (Article 33) — scope
rubrics_metrics.description: State debts are defined as financial obligations of a predecessor state arising in conformity with international law towards another state, an international organisation or other subjects of international law — excluding private creditors under the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because article 33 excludes private creditors, the Vienna Convention as drafted would not cover debts owed to private parties; commentators (e.g., US Restatement) argue analogous rules probably should apply to private creditors in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local and localised debts pass to successor
rubrics_metrics.description: Debts contracted by local governmental bodies (local debts) or debts incurred by the central government for local projects (localised debts) pass to the successor state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customary law treats local debts as passing to the successor because they are tied to the transferred territory; this is strengthened where the territory was fiscally autonomous.

rubrics_metrics.name: General (central) state debts — presumption of predecessor responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no clear rule for general state debts; the presumption is that the predecessor state remains responsible, particularly where only part of a state separates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice is sparse; historical examples (Ottoman Public Debt, post-partition India/Pakistan) suggest predecessor often remains liable. However, equitable apportionment has been done in some cases (e.g., UK/Irish Free State).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secured debts tied to territorial assets survive transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Debts secured by mortgage or other security over assets located in the territory (dettes hypothéquées) generally survive the transfer of that territory and remain enforceable against the asset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article examples and the Austrian Peace Treaty practice support survival of mortgages on local assets. By contrast, debts merely related to sources of income (dettes hypothecaires) may not follow the territory in the same way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 40 equitable apportionment approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 40 provides that when part of a state becomes another state, state debt passes to the successor 'in an equitable proportion' taking into account property, rights and interests which pass to the successor in relation to that debt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 40 may not be a codification of customary international law, but it reflects a plausible, theoretically grounded approach for apportioning general debts. Its applicability depends on parties' agreement and specific circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible bases for apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: Apportionment of debt or liabilities can be based on various criteria, including taxation ratio, extent of territory, population, nationality of creditors, taxable value, actual revenue contributions, value of assets, and contributions to central administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appropriate basis depends on the parties and circumstances; equitable solutions often use multi-year averages (value over several years) rather than single-year snapshots. The Commission's suggested fiscal criterion (20-year average federal revenues collected in Québec) is one acceptable basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of debts to private creditors in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Vienna Convention's definition excludes private creditors, authoritative commentators (US Restatement) consider the same apportionment rules that apply to interstate debts likely apply to private creditors as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States have in practice made arrangements covering private creditor obligations (e.g., UK/Irish Free State arrangements); negotiators should address private creditor liabilities explicitly in agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pension liabilities — general vs local distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Pensions accruing before the change of sovereignty generally constitute a charge upon the predecessor state; pensions payable by local treasuries (local administrative debt) pass to the successor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the central government was the employer, pension claims are enforceable against that central organ (predecessor). Where employment and pension obligations were managed and funded by local administrative units absorbed by the successor, those obligations pass to the successor. Parties may agree different arrangements (e.g., UK/Irish Free State treaty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance of assets and debts rooted in the territory
rubrics_metrics.description: Assets and debts that are rooted in the territory of the seceding unit (immovable property, local funds, localised debts) have special significance and are more readily allocated to the successor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The territorial dimension is dominant in practice; evaluators should not overlook assets/debts physically or legally linked to the territory when designing apportionment schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of fiscal-criteria based valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuation methods based on fiscal criteria (e.g., percentage of federal revenues collected in Québec averaged over 20 years) are an acceptable basis for allocating shares of financial assets and net value, subject to agreement by the federal government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission's proposed method (share of federal debt assumed equals share of overall assets; use of 20-year revenue average for financial assets/net value; non-financial assets by location ratio; pensions by proportion of federal employees resident in Québec) is consistent with international law principles provided the predecessor accepts it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of state practice and doctrinal opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: State practice and academic/doctrinal opinion are valuable in interpreting and applying international-law rules on succession where the law is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many norms are general and unclear, practice (e.g., UK/Irish 1921, India/Pakistan 1947) and doctrine (Brownlie, O'Connell, Shaw, US Restatement) inform possible solutions; negotiators should consider precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that succession occur in conformity with international law for Convention to apply
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vienna Conventions apply only to successions that occur in conformity with international law and particularly with principles incorporated in the UN Charter (e.g., not where succession results from unlawful annexation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 3 of the 1983 Convention and related instruments limit their scope to lawful successions; the legality of the secession process affects which international rules apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant territorialist approach with acknowledged uncertainties
rubrics_metrics.description: The dominant approach in international law is territorialist: property and debts closely linked to the territory pass to the successor, but uncertainties remain for movable property outside the territory and for general state debts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiators should recognise the territorial bias but also the lack of binding rules for some categories. A negotiated settlement addressing these grey areas is typical and advisable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of negotiation and agreement for many issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Many succession issues (valuation method, apportionment criteria, treatment of various debt classes) must be resolved through agreement between the predecessor and successor; parties are free to decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the flexibility in state practice and the contested status of some treaty provisions, a negotiated settlement is the practical and legal route to finalize the financial settlement. Expert advice and extended study may help develop acceptable formulas.
